newsitem.title: USA: U.S. incomes rose as 1996 ended but slowdown seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. incomes rose as 1996 ended but slowdown seen.

text.p: Consumers' incomes rose sharply as 1996 ended, the government said Monday, but industry was tempering hopes for economic growth in 1997 amid signs that manufacturing was slowing.

The Commerce Department said incomes from wages, salaries and all other sources rose 0.8 percent in December to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $6.64 trillion after rising 0.6 percent in November.
Personal incomes rose a solid 5.5 percent for all of 1996, though that was down from the 6.3 percent rise in 1995.

Spending on all types of goods and services increased 0.5 percent to a $5.27 trillion rate following a 0.4 percent rise in November, the department said. Consumer spending fuels about two-thirds of the nation's economy.

Separately, the National Association of Purchasing Management said its index of manufacturing activity fell to 52.0 in January from a revised 53.8 in December. A reading above 50 signals growth while one under that level points to contraction.

"Purchasing executives' comments on business conditions in January were less optimistic than in December, with many members describing business conditions as stable," said Norbert Ore, chairman of NAPM's Business Survey Committee and director of purchasing at Sonoco Products Co.

The group of purchasing executives, who buy wholesale supplies for factories, said manufacturing jobs fell for the 23rd consecutive month, although not as rapidly as they did in November, while new orders weakened and prices edged higher.

The reports came just before Federal Reserve policy-makers meet on Tuesday and Wednesday to plot interest-rate strategy. Analysts expect the central bankers to hold rates steady amid signs of solid economic growth but virtually no inflation.
Prices have remained well in check despite a pickup in growth in the fourth quarter, to a 4.7 percent annual rate from 2.1 percent in the third quarter.

Most analysts said the economy was already slowing from the brisk pace of growth late last year, and that the Fed has little evidence pointing to a pickup in inflation, though labor markets remain tight.

"Things are not overheating here by any means,' said economist Kathleen Stephansen of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York. "Inventories remained extraordinarily well contained."
Nor did analysts express concerns about a recession this year after uninterrupted growth since March 1991.

"All in all, the economy looks quite healthy, for two primary reasons," said Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers. "First, employment picked up quite a bit in the fourth quarter.
"Second, the massive appreciation of the stock market has raised household wealth, which permits additional spending."
In its report, the Commerce Department said more jobs helped boost December incomes.
"In December, employment, average weekly hours and average hourly earnings all increased," the department said.
Savings rose to 5.4 cents per dollar earned in December from 5.1 cents in November.

Spending on costly durable goods like new cars rose to an annual rate of $638.1 billion in December from $634.4 billion in November. Spending on nondurables edged up to $1.57 trillion from $1.56 trillion and spending for services was up to $3.05 trillion in December from $3.04 trillion.
The department also said spending on new construction fell in December for the first time in five months as government and private industry trimmed back on building projects.

Total spending on construction dropped 0.7 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $587.7 billion after a revised jump of 2 percent in November. It was the first drop since July when spending also fell 0.7 percent.
